title: Three chairs
hook: I had three chairs in my house: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society (Walden 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, companionable solitude: a rainy evening, and company found in the pattering of the drops. Your line was companionable solitude. Did you get some time alone, as good company? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

Three chairs. That's how a man known for living alone counts the seats in his small cabin. After a chapter praising solitude, Thoreau opens the very next one, Visitors, by saying he thinks he loves society as much as most. Then he tells us how his house was arranged for it, in one plain sentence: "I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society."
screen: `AFTER SOLITUDE, VISITORS.` → `HE LOVED SOCIETY TOO.` → `THREE CHAIRS.`

segments.voice: First, one chair. Solitude gets its own seat, and it comes first. That's yesterday's lesson, sitting quietly in the corner: being alone is a way of being in company too. Second, two chairs. Friendship needs exactly one more. Two people, facing each other, close enough to hear without raising a voice. Some of life's real conversations happen like this: across a kitchen table, in the front seats of a car, on a bench. Not in a crowd. Third, three chairs. Society, the wider world, still gets a place. Thoreau doesn't banish it. When more visitors came than he had chairs for, they stood, and he tells us with some pride how many people his small room could hold. A cabin, he suggests, is roomier than it looks when the guests are good company. Fourth, the room big thoughts need. Here's a lovely complaint. He writes: "One inconvenience I sometimes experienced in so small a house, the difficulty of getting to a sufficient distance from my guest when we began to utter the big thoughts in big words." He says big ideas need space to settle, like a bullet needing room to straighten out its flight, and so he and a friend would push their chairs back and back until they touched opposite walls. It's a joke, and it isn't. Some conversations need distance. Others need closeness. Three chairs is a quiet map of a whole life: room to be alone, room for one friend, and room for the world.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the second chair. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind one person you'd want in the chair across from you. Not a crowd. One. Let them sit down, in your mind. Notice how close the chairs are, and how it feels to have them there. What would you want to talk about, if there were no hurry? Let one real question come to you, the kind that needs two chairs. The bell holds the time.
Three chairs. Thoreau's furniture in Walden: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. A small map of room to be alone, room for a friend, and room for the world. Today's word.

Your line: three chairs. Today, have one two-chair conversation: just you and one other person, unhurried, with phones away. Ask the question that came to you. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden use the three chairs as a check on how their time is shared between being alone, time with one friend, and time with larger groups.

notes: Verify both quotations word for word against an 1854 text.

Paraphrases to check: 'I think that I love society as much as most'; when visitors came in larger numbers there was but the third chair for them all, but they generally economized the room by standing up; he says he had at one time a number of people under his roof (the script gives no number); the bullet image (thoughts must have room to settle into their last and steady course); pushing chairs back until they touched the wall in opposite corners.

Editor pass: cut the 'garden shed' comparison and the inaccurate 'furniture plan for guests' (the first chair is for solitude, not guests); 'as much as most people do' now matches the text's 'as much as most'; dropped the narrator's 'and a wise one'.
